title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) on the second postpartum day: learning experience from a case report and literature review
case_prompt:
A 31-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2 at 29 weeks 5 days of gestation, was transferred with severe preeclampsia complicated by HELLP syndrome. She denied prior hypertension or other illnesses. On presentation, her blood pressure was 200/120 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm, respiratory rate 23/min, SpO2 93% on room air (increased to 98% with 6–8 L/min oxygen), and temperature 37.0 °C. She complained of mild headache and epigastric pain but had normal vision. She had noted a productive cough with green sputum five days earlier. Pulmonary exam revealed decreased bronchial breath sounds with crackles and egophony. 

Laboratory tests showed thrombocytopenia (platelets 41×10^9/L), elevated LDH (2514 U/L), hyperuricemia (509 µmol/L), normal renal function otherwise, and proteinuria (3.0 g/L). White blood cell count was 15.06×10^9/L with 85.7% neutrophils. Chest radiography demonstrated patchy bilateral pulmonary opacifications without pleural effusion. Obstetric ultrasound revealed a small-for-gestational-age fetus and intra-abdominal fluid collections. 

She received intravenous nicardipine, magnesium sulfate, antibiotics, and underwent an emergent cesarean section for non-reassuring fetal heart rate. The neonate was delivered and transferred to the NICU. On postoperative day 2, her hemodynamics and labs stabilized except for anemia. On postoperative day 4, she developed headaches, altered sensorium, visual disturbance, and focal neurologic deficits. A neurologic consultation was obtained, and brain MRI was performed.
 
Brain MRI showed homogeneous low- to iso-signal intensity on T1-weighted images and diffuse symmetrical high-signal intensity lesions on T2-weighted and FLAIR images involving the white matter of the bilateral parieto-occipital lobes and lenticular nuclei. There was no mass lesion in the cerebellum or brainstem, and 3D-TOF MR angiography revealed no arteriovenous malformation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pneumonia was considered because “the patient had a cough symptom with green phlegm before the onset of hypertension” and “these changes suggested an infectious manifestation originated from the lung.”  
2. Acute pulmonary edema was considered in severe preeclampsia but excluded because “the SpO2 increased rapidly to 98% with oxygen support. This well-responded feature may be different from acute respiratory distress relating to pulmonary edema” and “the chest X-ray did not reveal an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the lung.”  
3. Eclampsia was considered given the context of severe preeclampsia and new neurologic deficits, but deemed unlikely because “the hypertension and laboratory tests were stable after the termination of pregnancy following the context of severe preeclampsia.”  
4. Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome was diagnosed based on MRI findings showing “diffuse symmetrical high-signal intensity lesions on T2 weighted image (T2WI) and T2 Flair involving white matters of bilateral parieto-occipital lobes and lenticular nucleus suggestive of PRES.”
